chapter_theme: A song at Thiruchakkarappalli (திருச்சக்கிரப்பள்ளி): hyperbole on the breasts of women who sell them, and a plea to be freed from attachment to their false union; the praise, in Sanskrit epithets, identifies Murugan with Sambandar, the king of Pugali, and the teacher of Agastya.

878.reading: The poet lists what the women's breasts do, outshine vessels, break golden pots, drive away the northern mountain, snap elephants' tusks, put bubbles to shame in a blink, rock lotuses in the field, send the paired birds into the sky, split tender coconuts, and asks when Murugan will grant that his mind's attachment to the false union and the hair of those who seal and sell those breasts will end. The praise, mostly in Sanskrit compounds, names Murugan the destroyer of the wicked who bears the shakti, master of the three Tamils, known by the name of the king of Pugali, the teacher who gave Agastya grammar in the south, the six-faced lord, who graced Parvati, she who grows the faiths, and rides the peacock at Seyppathi and dwells at Chakkarappalli, son of the three-eyed one.
878.nuance: முத்திரையிட்ட தனத்தை விற்பவர்: the breasts are sealed goods sold for money, which makes these courtesans. துட்கரக் கவிதைப் புகலிக் கரசு எனும் நாமம்: Murugan bears the name of the king of Pugali (Sirkazhi) of hard poems, that is Sambandar. சொல்லட்சண ... அகத்தியனுக்கருள் சொற்குரு: the teacher of grammar to Agastya. Some compounds in the praise are hard to divide.

links.note: 878 asks when his mind's attachment to the false union (பொய்க்கலவி) with women who seal and sell their breasts (முத்திரையிட்ட தனத்தை விற்பவர்) will end. Kural 913 calls the embrace of women of wealth false (பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) and likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. The song's பொய்க்கலவி is the Kural's பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், and both tie the falsehood to the sale.
